title: Self-Hosted AI Workflow Automation: A 2026 Guide
summary: Deploying these systems on private servers ensures complete control over sensitive data and operational logic without relying on third-party cloud…
body_markdown:
## Infrastructure requirements for private AI deployments


A hardware-first strategy is required for private AI deployments, where Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) capacity and local container orchestration replace the elastic scaling of public clouds.


This shift ensures that sensitive data never exits the internal network, but it places the burden of resource allocation directly on the local infrastructure team.


### GPU VRAM requirements for Llama 3.1


Local model performance is strictly gated by GPU memory. The choice of model size dictates the specific server hardware procurement.


According to PowerGPU, the Llama 3.1 8B model requires 18 GB of VRAM at 16-bit precision. This fits within a single consumer-grade or entry-level professional GPU.


**150 GB is required** when scaling to the 70B model, necessitating a multi-GPU node or a specialized server rack to handle the weights, effectively limiting your deployment options to high-end enterprise hardware, so you must account for significant infrastructure overhead.


The flagship 405B model demands 907 GB of VRAM, making it impossible to run on a single standard GPU, by which point you are forced to distribute the workload across a cluster of interconnected devices.


An organization must deploy a cluster of high-end enterprise H100 or A100 GPUs just to load the model into memory.


### Software: Container orchestration and model serving


By containerizing the logic and the models, a sovereign stack ensures they remain portable and isolated from the public internet.


The lifecycle of the automation engine and the model server is managed by Docker or Kubernetes, allowing for reproducible deployments across air-gapped environments.


Ollama or vLLM act as the inference engine, serving the LLM via a local API so that no data is sent to external providers like OpenAI.


To keep the entire logic flow behind the firewall, the n8n orchestration tool connects the local model to internal databases and applications.


In the following diagram, a local server rack is illustrated where the orchestration engine and Ollama reside behind a corporate firewall with no outbound traffic.


This setup ensures that even if a user prompts a model with trade secrets, the data packet physically cannot leave the local area network. Physical hardware, rather than a third-party service level agreement, defines the security perimeter.


### Security: Managing secrets in a non-cloud environment


The responsibility for protecting database credentials and API keys shifts from cloud-native vaults to local secret management in a private deployment. Without a managed service like AWS Secrets Manager, teams must use local environment variables or self-hosted instances of HashiCorp Vault.


> Physical hardware, rather than a third-party service level agreement, defines the security perimeter.


This prevents the "hard-coding" of credentials within automation workflows. It ensures that an auditor can verify that sensitive access tokens are encrypted at rest and never logged in plain text during execution.
